headline: What’s in
the shot.
dek: B12, lipo and MIC injections are sold for energy. The trials are few, or none.
byline: Adonis Men’s Health · Checked Oct 31, 2026 · Clinical review pending

glance.label: B12 for energy
glance.line: Two small placebo-controlled trials. Neither found a difference from placebo.

glance.label: MIC blends
glance.line: Compounded, not FDA approved. No published human study of injected M, I or C for energy.

glance.label: Ashwagandha
glance.line: A US supplement; illegal to sell as a food in Denmark.

body: The energy shot is one of the most familiar offers in men’s health: a quick injection, usually built around [[/vitamin-b12|vitamin B12]], promised to lift a tired week. Often it is sold as an MIC or lipotropic blend, named for the [[/methionine|methionine]], [[/inositol|inositol]] and [[/choline|choline]] it contains, sometimes with [[/vitamin-b6|vitamin B6]] or [[/l-carnitine|L-carnitine]] added. These blends are made by compounding pharmacies, and compounded drugs are not FDA approved; FDA does not review them for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold.[^compq]

B12 itself has a narrow approved job. The label for cyanocobalamin injection says it “is indicated for vitamin B 12 deficiencies due to malabsorption,”[^b12] and goes on to list the conditions that cause poor absorption, starting with pernicious anemia.[^b12] Feeling tired is not on that list. Injecting B12 for energy in someone whose B12 levels are normal is off-label.

The research on B12 shots for energy in people who are not deficient is thin, and what exists does not favor the shot. In a randomized, double-blind crossover trial, 20 professional singers with mild voice symptoms such as fatigue received one B12 injection and one salt-water injection, weeks apart.[^singers] The authors found “no meaningful difference compared with placebo.”[^singers] An older trial gave 15 people with chronic fatigue syndrome injections of liver extract, folic acid and B12, or a placebo, in a crossover design.[^kaslow] “Although patients responded to placebo and LEFAC by several criteria of functional status, no significant difference was apparent between response to placebo and that to LEFAC,”[^kaslow] the authors wrote, adding: “The placebo response appeared to be strong.”[^kaslow] LEFAC was the name of the active injection. Both trials were small, and neither tested the multi-ingredient blends that men are usually offered today, so even this modest evidence speaks only to B12 on its own.

For the other ingredients the record is thinner still. We found no published human study of injected methionine, inositol or choline, alone or in a blend, for energy or fat loss. FDA’s drug records list no approved methionine product and no approved inositol product.[^methfda][^inosfda] Vitamin B6 and L-carnitine are approved drugs, but for other purposes. The pyridoxine injection label says the injected route “is indicated when oral administration is not feasible as in anorexia, nausea and vomiting, and preoperative and postoperative conditions,”[^b6] in people with B6 deficiency. The Carnitor label approves levocarnitine for carnitine deficiency, not for energy.[^carnitor] Most studies of L-carnitine and weight used supplements taken by mouth.

Then there is the question of how the shots are made. FDA’s recall records list many compounded lipotropic, Lipo-B and MIC injections recalled by the pharmacies that made them. A 2016 recall of a lipotropic injection containing L-carnitine and methylcobalamin, a form of B12, gave the reason as “Lack of Assurance of Sterility.”[^recalls] That phrase appears again and again in the records for these products.[^recalls] Sterility matters more for an injection than for a pill, because the product goes directly into the body.

None of this means B12 is useless. People who are truly deficient need it, and the injection is the approved treatment when the gut cannot absorb it.[^b12] The point is narrower: the shot sold as a general pick-me-up has very little evidence behind it, and the blends sold alongside it have almost none. Even the approved injection is not risk-free. Its label warns that “anaphylactic shock and death have been reported after parenteral vitamin B 12 administration,”[^b12] and recommends a small test dose under the skin first.[^b12] Parenteral means given by injection rather than by mouth.

The other popular energy product in this lane is not a shot at all. [[/ashwagandha|Ashwagandha]], the root of Withania somnifera, is sold in the US as a dietary supplement, and FDA says it “does not have the authority to approve dietary supplements before they are marketed.”[^suppqa] The agency adds that, generally, “a firm does not have to provide FDA with the evidence it relies on to substantiate safety before or after it markets its products.”[^suppqa] Ashwagandha is marketed for stress, energy and testosterone. Its trials are small and short. In one randomized, double-blind crossover trial in 57 overweight men aged 40 to 70 with mild fatigue, an extract raised testosterone 14.7% more than placebo over eight weeks, “although no significant between-group differences were found in cortisol, estradiol, fatigue, vigor, or sexual well-being.”[^lopresti]

Ashwagandha also has a safety record that its marketing rarely mentions. A case series from Iceland and the US Drug-Induced Liver Injury Network described five people with liver injury after taking it.[^bjornsson] The authors concluded that “these cases illustrate the hepatotoxic potential of ashwagandha,”[^bjornsson] and that the injury was “typically cholestatic or mixed with severe jaundice and pruritus, but self-limited with liver tests normalizing in 1-5 months.”[^bjornsson] Hepatotoxic means harmful to the liver.

One country has gone further. Denmark’s food agency says ashwagandha may not be sold as a food there, including in supplements and drinks, citing a 2020 risk assessment by the Danish technical university’s food institute.[^dk][^dtu] That assessment looked at animal studies that showed effects on sex hormones and reproduction in male rats, and on the thyroid.[^dtu] In the US, it remains on store shelves as a supplement.

What is still unknown is simple to state. No good trial has shown that B12 shots raise energy in people with normal B12, no human study has tested what the MIC blends do, and the long-term safety of ashwagandha in men has not been studied in large trials. For athletes, none of these is named on the World Anti-Doping Agency’s list, but large intravenous infusions are banned as a method.[^wada]
